question: A 22-year-old woman presents with her third episode of cystitis in 6 months. Urine culture grows E. coli expressing P fimbriae. Which of the following best explains the predominant route of infection in this patient?

answers.text: Ascending colonisation from perineal flora via the urethra to the bladder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ascending route accounts for >95% of UTIs. Faecal E. coli colonise the perineum, ascend via the short female urethra (4 cm), and adhere to bladder uroepithelium using P fimbriae that bind glycolipid receptors on uroepithelial cells.

answers.text: Haematogenous seeding from a distant focus of bacteraemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haematogenous spread accounts for <5% of UTIs and typically causes renal cortical abscesses in the setting of bacteraemia (e.g., infective endocarditis) — it does not explain recurrent cystitis in a young woman.

answers.text: Lymphatic spread from the gastrointestinal tract to the bladder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lymphatic spread is a rare theoretical route proposed in severe bowel disease. It does not explain the common pattern of recurrent cystitis in young women.

answers.text: Direct extension from an adjacent infected pelvic organ

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direct extension requires an anatomical defect such as a vesicovaginal fistula or diverticular abscess — none of which is present in this otherwise healthy young woman.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the routes of UTI infection. The ascending route from perineal flora via the urethra accounts for >95% of UTIs, particularly in women, and is facilitated by uropathogenic virulence factors such as P fimbriae.

The ascending route — faecal flora → perineum → urethra → bladder — is the predominant mechanism of UTI, especially in women. The short female urethra and proximity of the urethral meatus to the anus facilitate bacterial ascent.
